title: Loading a table with pandas

cells.text: **pandas** is the Python tool for working with tables. Before you can use it, you **import** it. Everyone gives it the short name `pd`, so you type less. Then `pd.read_csv()` loads a CSV file into a table called a **DataFrame**, which analysts usually name `df`.

cells.prompt: Press Run to import pandas, load games.csv into df, and show it.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
df

cells.text: Each **row** is one game, and each **column** is one detail about it. The bold numbers on the left are row labels, and pandas starts counting at **0**, not 1. Writing `df` on the last line of a cell shows the table.
Real tables can have thousands of rows, so analysts peek at the start with `df.head()`. The empty brackets mean "use the default number of rows".

cells.prompt: How many rows will df.head() show? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: Put a number in the brackets to choose how many rows to show. For example, `df.head(2)` shows the first 2 rows.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with a number so only the first 3 rows show, then press Run.
hints: Type just the number, without quotes.

cells.text: `df.tail()` works the same way, but shows the **last** rows instead of the first.

cells.prompt: Which row will df.tail(1) show? Pick one, then press Run.
Your turn. The cell already starts with df. for you. Finish it using tail() so it shows the last 2 rows, then press Run.
hints: Type tail with a number inside the brackets, right after df.

recap: import pandas as pd, then pd.read_csv() loads a table into df. head() shows the first rows and tail() shows the last. Rows are counted from 0.
